## CUDA public merge 20261024 1024

https://www.kaggle.com/code/lightningv08/squares-in-squares-cuda-packing-search

# Public notebook narrative and source attribution

## 1. Where the gain comes from

For each n, keep the smallest independently certified container. The metric is the sum of **L / sqrt(n) − 1** over n = 1,…,1000. Omitted puzzles receive the official grid score.

The new public union retains 13 complementary witnesses from Sung Heo's pinned dashboard and 45 from Dariush Afshar's newer construction output. Kirill's Edge LP output adds no further wins after that union. Dariush's 45 rows are labelled `construction` in his source table; their gain belongs to his search. Earlier mathematical construction and witness credits remain attached.

The next stages are independent implementations tested here. Counts are accepted stage replacements and may include the same n twice. Stage gains are sequential accounting, not a causal ablation.

## 5. Readable source and optional recomputation

The following archive restores the exact readable Python and CUDA C++ source, credited geometry helpers and unchanged official metric. SHA256 guards the archive and all frozen inputs. Default execution needs NumPy, pandas, SciPy, matplotlib and a compatible mpmath. The optional CUDA branch also needs CuPy, PyTorch and an NVIDIA driver with NVRTC; the Kaggle GPU image supplies this stack. CPU replay does not import CUDA libraries.

Enable `RECOMPUTE_LP` for a bounded 24-layout dual-guided pass or `RECOMPUTE_CUDA` for the 32-bin CUDA composition. Each starts from the frozen best, and admission is monotone. GPU memory is checked before allocating the profile table; this configuration needs approximately 6 GB free device memory. Results may vary with finite solver budgets and numerical libraries. The frozen default CSV is byte-exact.

## Prior portfolio notices

# Alternating CPU Contact Reclosure

Pinned baseline: avazaku, Squarecraft II | Unjam the Grid, version 2, native 361225541.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/avazaku/squarecraft-ii-unjam-the-grid-22-408597-lb?scriptVersionId=361225541
Baseline CSV SHA256 b44144246654affdee31949aa47e3d52eea95cdad574984bd1bf5c7b03ef8559.
The nine improvements over our previous public version, including n984 and n553, are credited to avazaku. His binary contact-switch experiment informed this follow-up. The new experiment alternates our CPU separation graph LP with free-angle contact refinement, rebuilding the graph after each relaxation. Fixed-angle separation choices are sampled, not solved by a new MILP. Every admitted witness retains exact unit square sizes and is certified using the unchanged official v17 metric. This incremental experiment makes no invention or global-optimality claim.
All new search ran on CPU; no CUDA or MPS was used. The default notebook restores the frozen result, exports readable search source and logs, then evaluates raw CSV decimals and a default pandas float64 round trip. It does not rerun optimization.

## Previous public source notices

# CPU Rectangular Reclosure

Primary baseline: Chris Deotte (cdeotte), Squares in Squares L-Cut GPU Squeeze 22.41, version 1, native version 361208974.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/cdeotte/squares-in-squares-l-cut-gpu-squeeze-22-41?scriptVersionId=361208974

A complementary public input is Kirill's CPU Separation Graph Reclosure version 8 (native 361188237), with its inherited authors and notices retained below.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-472940-cpu-separation-graph-reclosure?scriptVersionId=361188237

This release applies bounded fixed-angle separating-axis linear programs to the new layouts, then free-angle CPU contact refinement and complete translated-window subset propagation at 0/45 degrees. These are incremental experiments with prior algorithmic lineage, not claims to invent packing LPs. cpu_contact_polish.py is adapted from lightningv08 under Apache 2.0; its notice is retained. All new search ran on CPU. No GPU or MPS used. Unit squares retain side length one; clearance is introduced by centre displacement only. The unchanged official metric v17 certifies actual CSV decimals and a default pandas round trip. No global optimality claim is made.
# CPU Separation Graph Reclosure

Frozen baseline: kozykappa, Subset transfer, contact refinement and centre compaction,
version 1, native 361161040.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/kozykappa/subset-transfer-contact-refinement-and-compaction?scriptVersionId=361161040
CSV SHA256: f0478afdf71c02e57c0852c6bdcb510802677ce76bfd6ec1c56375a6e01ec1c5.

The frozen portfolio and complementary fault-line merge are credited to kozykappa
and the inherited authors in the retained notices. This release measures only
its gain over that stronger starting point, rather than the older Kirill V7.
The main experiment selects among currently valid separating axes at contacts
and solves a bounded, fixed-angle LP for all square centres and the box side.
Alternative separation choices permit different row motions. It then applies
CPU free-angle contact refinement and integer-border/subset propagation.
Linear-programming packing and separating-axis constraints have prior lineage;
this is a reproducible incremental experiment, not a claim to invent them.
cpu_contact_polish.py is adapted from lightningv08's Apache-2.0 implementation.
The new cpu_axis_reclosure.py and experiment runners are readable source.
All search used Apple M5 Pro CPU; no CUDA, MPS or GPU was used.
Unit-square sizes never change. Final admission uses the unchanged official v17
metric (Apache 2.0), on both direct decimals and a default pandas float64 round trip.
The standard 0/45-degree transfer pass was also tested before the new LP pass;
its negative result remains in the logs. No global-optimality claim is made.

NOTICE.content:
fq: fast smooth quench for unit-square packings
Copyright (c) 2026 Evan Daniel. MIT license in LICENSE.
Source: https://github.com/evand/square-packing
Pinned commit:659ee62e4a9d39542a1146e8b011cc3ab6407ede

The Rust sources are unchanged. The local Cargo manifest selects only fq.
The original source credits Nakajima and Ostashev for soft-to-rigid search.
Its floating-point feasibility output is a search proposal; this repository
independently checks raw and numeric-roundtrip geometry with Kaggle metric17.

inherited_parent_additional_provenance.scope: Two original-reference native improvements. All twelve control inputs, native returns, raw/decoded/certified poses, logs and source snapshots are retained. No GPU-initializer attribution. Exact inherited source notices and ancestry retained. Export performs no optimization, geometry certification, scaling or coordinate reserialization.

public_source_provenance.certificate_scope: All18 source cases passed unchanged original-decimal raw official, ordinary default-pandas official and independent interval gates. Future merged portfolio requires its own complete official/transport checks. No geometry transformation performed.

public_certification_summary.scope: Changed source cases only; root owns full merged portfolio, transport-safe proof and canonical pointer. No submission or canonical mutation.

CSV SHA2568b4f69633ce481ffe85e257451b57f91f4f1cc2bcc26ea35a60d299371031048 . Reviewed latest metadata sourceV18; scored V17 output separately pinned. New inherited gains include gadget quench using Evan Daniel fq, ranked non-exact cropped gadgets and Chris Deotte-inspired fault-line DP. Francisco Couzo exact witnesses and all original authors retain credit. No downloaded Rust/shell code executed.

Our frozen Wide LP V13/native361366472 contributes complementary witnesses, SHA2560463c584b29b96427ff56a9f328bf18f9c85a1f631b2ba5bd19e752eca9a4555. CPU fixed-axis scan seed317811+n, trust .45, tie .2. Quarter-turn snap pilot inspired by Yang Kuang Ou workbench V5/native361384699 (Apache2.0), whose historical n376 effect motivated our independent implementation in run_round15_snap.py. Three targets, three thresholds, same starts; null and harmful arms retained. This is not a new LP algorithm or a general causal claim.

CPU default tested; CUDA/MPS genuine optional proposals retained but hardware untested. Official metric unchanged; actual raw and ordinary pandas roundtrip certified. All1000 terms remain, grid-equivalent groups use official fallback.

# Wide contact graph + complementary frontier

Primary input: Alex Chilton, Fault-line DP + Basin Hopping V13/native361349910, stable notebook ID140171258.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/alexchilton/fault-line-dp-basin-hopping-lb-22-3747?scriptVersionId=361349910
CSV SHA256ebd3da2157fc55663b4240fce19a3269fba95b5ff2bf97c771bb6cd11d60f21f, fresh unchanged-metric score22.374684483947835. It carries rational witnesses, Evan Daniel's credited basin-hopping engine, Deotte-inspired fault DP and public merges; no inherited discovery is attributed to our release. The source cells were reviewed, not executed. Its public page identifies V13 and Apache2.0. A metadata pull can expose newer V14 with the same source cells; version13 output is explicitly pinned.

Our own public V12/native361359846 contributes complementary graph/contact witnesses. That version locally certified22.374688280983825, but was not submitted because a fresh check showed Alex V13 had moved ahead. No attempt was consumed. A wider fixed-angle scan starts from these V12 witnesses (trust0.65, tie0.4, seed244949+n). Per-size selection merges the best source and wide candidates, then quantization, centre-only clearance and full official raw/pandas certification decide final admission. The prior matched L1 pilot showed no advantage and is not claimed as the cause of current gain.

The new EDA measures interaction-pair counts under three trust radii on the same input geometry and distinguishes complementary source gain from the final increment. It is descriptive, not a speed or causal benchmark. We export545 improved witnesses and use the explicitly permitted grid fallback for455 grid-equivalent sizes, retaining all1000 score contributions. Omitting exact grid groups is not counted as an optimization gain.

CPU/CUDA/MPS tensor proposal paths are retained with CPU default. Exact LP and certification run on CPU for all modes. CPU tested; CUDA/MPS configured but not hardware-tested; local MPS was not used. Unit squares stay unit-sized and the official metric is unchanged. Stable-ID resolution plus version and SHA256 checks protect public input downloads against title changes.

# Matched L1 Contact LP: provenance and limits

Frozen primary input is our public Donor Contact LP V11, notebook140109166/native361331790.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-3747-cpu-cuda-mps-eda-donor-lp?scriptVersionId=361331790
CSV SHA256ebee94f678faf861d40f246a48d50bdb2c87c79020907f74ae052ae2416d2ece. It was freshly certified in that release; the identical hash-bound report is retained as the baseline evidence. Its much larger inherited quality and all original discoverers are credited below.

Aqib Raza's V10 public blend, native361349660, moved ahead by approximately1.52e-8 in the catalog. Its source blends our output and other public files, including float64 roundtrip variants, with a fast floating SAT screen. That screen is not our certificate and is not used here. We reviewed its methods and credits but run independent CPU experiments from our exact already-verified own V11 input. Final publication requires an actual certified score materially below the current public leader, not just a cosmetic representation change.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/aqibrazadev/squares-in-squares-top-lb-blending-visualization?scriptVersionId=361349660

Our new experiment follows a full bounded randomized separation-graph scan with paired free-angle contact LP arms. One minimizes side length; the other adds a small L1 absolute-motion penalty1e-5 to the same existing LP formulation. They start from the same coordinates/seeds with equal nominal budgets. Actual wall times and iterations can differ, so this is a finite descriptive paired experiment rather than a universal causal or speed claim. Independent full geometry, quantized decimals and the unchanged official metric decide admission. We never assume a positive effect of regularization before seeing the paired results.

CPU/CUDA/MPS proposal modes remain real; CPU default. Exact LP and metric run on CPU in every mode. CPU was tested; CUDA/MPS configured but not hardware-tested. The local MPS device was not used. Final unit-square sides remain one; only centres are repaired for clearance. Raw and pandas float64 roundtrip are independently certified. No metric tolerances are changed and no mathematical-record claim is made.

# CPU Donor LP over CUDA Packing Search V14

Pinned primary numerical input: Vladislav Lavrentev (lightningv08), CUDA Packing Search V14, native361328545.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/lightningv08/squares-in-squares-cuda-packing-search?scriptVersionId=361328545
CSV SHA256368e4d5f9ea6008792fe51bdd1aeba4108572361268145d8cffe451a65ce7223.
V14 refreshes public witnesses from Chris Deotte Ensemble V1 and own Contact Atlas V9, then searches neighbouring deletion starts, coherent CUDA relaxation, CPU contact LP and donor recomposition. Its inherited starting quality is not credited to this new release.

This release merges complementary own V10 witnesses, runs a finite CPU boundary-deletion beam for n+1/+2/+3 followed by fresh graph reclosure, and alternates free-angle contact refinement on six scan targets. The deletion idea is credited to Malyshev Danil and lightningv08 V14; our finite beam implementation is independent. Stage logs and EDA show whether direct deletions actually contributed. Measured gain is incremental over the complete pinned V14 CSV; sequential stage gains overlap and are not a causal benchmark.

CPU/CUDA/MPS tensor proposal modes are retained, CPU default; float64 geometry/LP and unchanged official metric always run on CPU. CPU code was tested, CUDA/MPS configured but not hardware-tested. No MPS/GPU was allocated for this release. Final witnesses are unit squares with centre-only clearance repair, fixed-point decimals and independent raw plus pandas roundtrip certification. No optimum or mathematical record claim.

Primary frozen input: Chris Deotte (cdeotte), Squares in Squares Ensemble 22.376, version 1, native 361320805.

Finite wall budgets and fixed seeds are recorded; no optimum, new mathematical record or cross-device speed claim is made.

Frozen primary baseline: Vladislav Lavrentev (lightningv08), Squares in Squares | CUDA Packing Search, version 13, native 361296742.
https://www.kaggle.com/code/lightningv08/squares-in-squares-cuda-packing-search?scriptVersionId=361296742
CSV SHA256 ce991f2abcfeb3ed0abfe20ea022cea43470f9a916985f623f1cebf2d5dce1cc.
V13 incorporates our V5 witnesses, complementary Janus D4 witnesses, coherent CUDA restarts, bounded graph changes and donor recomposition. Its numerical coordinates are inherited and credited in full. The exact V13 source notices and supporting reports are retained under source_provenance/.

Our increment rebuilds valid separation-axis graphs on the refreshed V13 witnesses and alternates centre compaction with free-angle contact refinement on the strongest new opportunities. A separate ten-puzzle pilot of sampled binary contact switching, inspired by Squarecraft II, produced no material admitted gain; that negative control is retained and is not credited with the result. The portable exploratory implementation offers CPU/CUDA/MPS tensor proposals, with exact CPU geometry, LP and official certification in all modes. CPU implementation and gradients were tested in the prior V5 release; CUDA/MPS remain configured but not hardware-tested. This release's new measured improvement comes from CPU graph and contact LP, not a GPU experiment.

The default run restores pinned inputs and fixed-point new witnesses, then freshly certifies raw decimals and a default pandas float64 round trip. RUN_SEARCH enables optional recomputation on the selected backend. MPS requires a local Mac and is unavailable on Kaggle. Square side lengths stay one; only centres move for numerical clearance. No optimality or algorithm-invention claim is made.

## 5. Recompose the updated gadgets on CUDA

A crop with footprint w×h and surplus d contains w·h+d unit squares in a box (w+f)×(h+f). Along a staircase fault, several such gadgets add their surpluses while sharing a container excess controlled by the **largest f**. Reusing a better donor can therefore improve multiple puzzles.

CUDA C++ computes crop order statistics, conservative separating-line tip profiles and the minimax DAG search. # Fault-line DP + Basin Hopping

Four steps beyond merging public notebooks:

1. **Couzo's certified register.** Francisco Couzo keeps exact (rational) packings for n = 1 … 10,000 at
   [github.com/franciscouzo/square-packing](https://github.com/franciscouzo/square-packing) (MIT), many of them
   records above n = 324 that no public notebook had. We convert them and keep each one only if the official metric
   certifies it after a float64 round trip.
2. **Search.** Basin hopping with Evan Daniel's Rust engine from
   [github.com/evand/square-packing](https://github.com/evand/square-packing) (`search/packer`, MIT), started from
   our current packings of the puzzles above 324 that are still plain 0°/45° constructions.
3. **Fault-line gadget DP.** Our rebuild of Chris Deotte's composition: crops of the best packings (including the hop
   results) become gadgets along a fault between two shifted lattices, so one local improvement is reused in many n.
4. **Gadget quench.** Squeeze the gadgets themselves with Evan Daniel's smooth solver `fq` (same repository): loosen
   the gadget's box a little, nudge the squares, squeeze it again. A smaller gadget lowers every puzzle that uses it.

Builds on *Thinking Outside the Grid* (the problem, the float64 trap, the 45° family) and
*Certified Merge of Public Packings* (whose output is the starting point here).

## 0. Every known method on one page

The score is the sum over n = 1 … 1000 of L_n/√n − 1, so every puzzle counts, and a gain on a big n is worth as much
as the same relative gain on a small one. These are the methods that move it, roughly in the order they were found.
The column *here* says where this notebook uses each one.

| method | idea in one line | from | here |
|---|---|---|---|
| grid | ⌈√n⌉ × ⌈√n⌉ upright squares; the fallback for every puzzle | — | baseline |
| tilt a square (Göbel 1979) | n = k² + 1: four corner blocks plus squares turned 45° in the middle beat the next grid size | Göbel, Ellsworth's enumerator | starting point |
| record tables | best-known packings for all n ≤ 324 and some larger | Friedman, Ellsworth, Couzo | §1 |
| merge | take the smallest certified box per n from every public notebook | everyone | §3 |
| closures | delete squares from a smaller-box packing of n + k (L_n ≤ L_{n+k}); add an L of squares to n − m | standard | §3 |
| basin hopping | fix the box, minimise overlap with L-BFGS, kick, accept by Metropolis, shrink when overlap-free | Evan Daniel's `packer` | §2 |
| contact LP reclosure | freeze angles, choose a separating axis per touching pair, solve one LP for all centres and the box | Kirill, kozykappa, lightningv08 | inputs |
| fault-line gadget DP | cut good packings into w × h gadgets and chain them along a seam between two shifted lattices | Chris Deotte | §4 |
| gadget quench | squeeze the gadgets the DP uses most, then rerun the DP | this notebook, after Deotte's GPU squeeze | §4b |
| L-cuts | remove a strip from a bigger gadget and re-squeeze it into a smaller key | Chris Deotte (GPU) | not here |

And one trap that silently costs points: the metric reads the CSV as float64 and certifies with interval arithmetic,
so squares that touch *exactly* (any construction with √2 in it) fail. Every packing here is scaled by 1 + 1e-12
about its centre before it is written, which turns contacts into gaps that survive the round trip.

## 1. Couzo's witnesses

Each `.cert` file is an exact packing: the first line is `n side`, then one line per square `x y t` as rationals,
with the rotation stored as `t = tan(θ/2)` so that cos and sin stay rational. Exact packings touch exactly, which the
official metric cannot certify after float64 rounding, so `couzo.py` converts them with 40-digit arithmetic and scales
each packing by 1 + 1e-12 about its centre. Converted file: `couzo.csv` in the starter-kit dataset.

## 2. Basin hopping

`packer hop` keeps the box side fixed and minimises the total overlap (separating-axis penetration, as in the metric)
with L-BFGS. Every step it perturbs a few squares (shift, rotate, swap) and accepts the result by a Metropolis rule.
Whenever the packing becomes overlap-free it **squeezes** the box and sets the next target just below the best side
found, so a run only ever goes down.

Starting points matter: the 0°/45° constructions are rigid and symmetric, and a few minutes of hopping often finds
a slightly tilted, slightly smaller relative. We build the engine here (needs *internet on*) and run a short live
demo; the bigger runs were done offline with the same code (`hop_search.py`), results in `hop.csv`.

## 3. Merge everything

## 4. Fault-line gadget DP

Idea from Chris Deotte's *multi-gadget fault DP* notebook (his markdown describes it; his notebook ships the packings, not the code,
so `fault_dp.py` is our rebuild). Write n = K² + D. Fill the lower-left of a box with upright unit cells on the integer lattice
and the upper-right with the same lattice shifted by f in x and y. The two "continents" meet along a staircase fault running
down the anti-diagonal. Along the fault sit **gadgets**: w × h blocks that hold w·h + dm squares inside (w+f) × (h+f).
Every gadget adds dm squares; the box side is K + f, with f the largest overhang in the chain.

* **Gadgets are crops.** Take any good packing (ours, Couzo's up to n = 3500, the hop results), under each of its 8 symmetries,
  and for every (w, h, dm) keep the w·h + dm squares that stick out least past w × h: that order statistic is f.
* **Seams.** Two gadgets meet corner to corner (only if the tips cannot collide), or with one lattice column or row between them.
* **DP** over (columns used, rows used, surplus, tip type of the last gadget), minimising the largest f.
  A gadget that basin hopping improved in one puzzle is then reused in every band that can hold it.
* Each composition is certified with the official metric after the float64 round trip before it is used.

## 4b. Gadget quench

The DP only rearranges gadgets it already has, so its result is limited by how tight each gadget is.
Here we make the gadgets themselves tighter.

**Quench** is a squeeze. Take a gadget (say 7 × 17 cells holding 130 squares, sticking out by f = 0.90174),
make its box 0-4 % looser, nudge every square a little (about 0.01 in position, a fraction of a degree in angle), then
shrink the box as far as it goes without any overlap. Evan Daniel's `fq` does the shrinking: instead of pushing
overlapping squares apart, it gives every touching pair its own separating line and moves the lines too, which keeps
the problem smooth, so the optimiser does not stall at flat contacts. We repeat this from the best layout so far for
60 seconds per gadget and keep the best.

**Which gadgets.** Not all gadgets move. One built from an exact construction (f = (p + q√2)/r, e.g. Göbel's 8 × 8 + 1
at f = 0.5355) is rigid: every square is locked by contacts and every squeeze returns it unchanged. One found by a
numerical search is usually *almost* rigid: a few squares have a little slack, and a squeeze can win something.
So we target the 78 gadgets that the DP leans on most (ranked offline: lower one gadget's f by 0.005, rerun the DP, sum
the gains over all puzzles) and whose f is not such an exact value. Measured on our best file: 21 of them gave
15 smaller gadgets and +0.0015 over 29 puzzles; most of it came from long thin ones (7 × 16, 7 × 19, 5 × 18, 8 × 23).

Every improved gadget joins the DP's table; every new composition is certified with the official metric before it is used.

## 5. Official score

## 6. What we learned

* **Search rate.** A pilot of 24 construction puzzles × 5 CPU-minutes improved 4 of them, +0.000297 in total:
  about 1.5e-4 score per CPU-hour. Small per run, but there are ~220 such puzzles above n = 324 and nothing else is
  searching them.
* **The grid puzzles are not the target.** 457 puzzles are still the plain grid; for none of them is any smaller box
  known (checked against Couzo's register), and 144 are proven optimal (n = k², k² − 1 … k² − 4). They add the same
  ~7.36 to every team's score.
* **Composition multiplies search.** The fault DP turned hop results on single puzzles (e.g. n = 372, 451) into gadgets
  for larger puzzles: 47 more puzzles improved, +0.0021, from donors we already had. Re-running it on its own output
  gives +0.0002, then +0.0001: it converges in about three passes.
* **Gadgets beat puzzles.** Squeezing 21 gadgets for 60 s each gave +0.0015, about 0.004 score per CPU-hour:
  30-50 times what basin hopping on whole puzzles gives, because each gadget is reused across many puzzles.
* **Rigid gadgets do not move.** The biggest levers (8 × 8 + 1, 12 × 12 + 4, 16 × 16 + 9) are exact constructions;
  a squeeze returns them unchanged. Improving those needs a new construction, not more search.
* **What decides the leaderboard**: syncing new public records quickly (ties go to the earliest submission) and
  search on the non-grid puzzles above 324.

**What did not work** (measured on our files; each is a null, so you can skip it):

| tried | result |
|---|---|
| quench on exact-construction gadgets (8 × 8 + 1, 12 × 12 + 4, 16 × 16 + 9) | 0: they are rigid, every squeeze returns them unchanged |
| "cushion shift": move a gadget with f < F up or right inside its slot so more seams need no buffer | 0 gain at five values of F; chains above n = 324 have room for buffer seams |
| synthetic tilted-block gadgets (a turned a × b block in an upright grid) | 0.14 to 0.29 worse in f than cropped gadgets |
| a local LLM (30B coder) writing gadget constructors, then gadget searches | 0 new gadgets in about 1,600 programs; the plain squeeze loop it was meant to beat found them |

**Public notebooks whose outputs this notebook merges** (their packings are most of the score; thank you):

* [Кирилл Тымчишин (kirilltym)](https://www.kaggle.com/kirilltym): the contact-LP reclosure series (separation-graph, seam LP,
  donor LP, wide LP): fixed-angle LPs over separating axes that move whole rows of squares at once.
* [Vladislav Lavrentev (lightningv08)](https://www.kaggle.com/code/lightningv08/squares-in-squares-cuda-packing-search):
  CUDA packing search, deletion starts from neighbouring n, and the Apache-2.0 contact-polish code many notebooks build on.
* [Chris Deotte (cdeotte)](https://www.kaggle.com/cdeotte): multi-gadget fault DP, L-cut gadgets and GPU squeezing, and the ensemble.
* [Malyshev Danil (malyshevdanil)](https://www.kaggle.com/malyshevdanil): fresh certified records and neighbour transfer + squeeze.
* [kozykappa](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kozykappa/subset-transfer-contact-refinement-and-compaction): subset transfer, contact refinement and compaction.
* [SeshuRaju (seshurajup)](https://www.kaggle.com/seshurajup), [yuki16](https://www.kaggle.com/yuki16),
  [aqibrazadev](https://www.kaggle.com/aqibrazadev), [dariushafshar](https://www.kaggle.com/dariushafshar): ensembles, merges and validators.

*Credits: Chris Deotte (the fault-line gadget idea, and ranking gadgets by DP leverage), Francisco Couzo (certified register), Evan Daniel and contributors (evand/square-packing, packer and fq engines),
David Ellsworth (records, enumerator), Erich Friedman's survey, and the public notebooks merged in the starting point.
If this helped, an upvote is appreciated.*

SQUARECRAFT / EXPERIMENT 03

Seam Surgery

Find the stressed contacts. Unlock a neighbourhood. Certify the result.

A CPU search on a frozen public portfolio, with a separate measurement of our own incremental gain. This experiment uses LP shadow prices to focus mixed-integer contact changes near stressed seams. It is a heuristic for selecting a neighbourhood, not a global packing certificate. **Lower is better.** All 1,000 puzzle contributions are counted, with the competition grid fallback for omitted puzzles. The final exported CSV is evaluated by the unchanged official metric and again after a pandas float64 round trip. ## 1. What changed since Squarecraft II? The public portfolio progressed from 22.408597 to approximately 22.307847. New tilted-core mutation and exact upright refill methods produce different contact graphs. We inherit those witnesses with explicit credit, then test whether contact selection can improve them further. In Squarecraft II, binary choices were sampled at ambiguous contacts. Here a preliminary fixed-angle LP supplies constraint shadow prices. We score each candidate pair by its own pressure plus pressure on its endpoints. Half the binary budget goes to the highest scored pairs; the remainder is seeded random coverage. This targets a local contact neighbourhood while retaining exploration. Shadow prices can be unstable at degenerate optima, so no causal or optimality claim is made about this ranking. ## 2. Pinned public baseline and credit The starting CSV is kmmmvs, **Squares Dashboard Public Batch 20261024, version 11**, native notebook version 361781862. Both version and SHA-256 are pinned. The dashboard copies its public best-validated-packings dataset without running a solver. Its aggregate quality belongs to the credited contributors and original packing authors, not to this notebook. The published dataset's manifest, contributor table and provenance snapshots are preserved below. Earlier geometry helpers, official metric and inherited licenses are restored separately. The numeric baseline remains pinned even if the public dataset later changes. ## 3. Dual-guided contact surgery For each nearby pair, non-overlap requires at least one separating local axis. Freezing one axis makes centre compaction a linear program. Its shadow prices measure local objective sensitivity to those frozen constraints. We distribute these pressures to incident squares and use them to choose a bounded set of binary axis alternatives. The subsequent MILP optimizes all centres and the box side jointly. We test two trust radii and allow a small initial projection deficit on alternative axes in the second pass. Pair-specific big-M constants come from the movement bounds; a radius of $\sqrt2+2\sqrt2t$ covers all pairs that might collide. Every returned candidate is independently repaired and checked before admission. ## 4. Source provenance snapshot The public dataset can evolve independently of the pinned notebook CSV. These files document the retrieved source snapshot; their hashes are recorded. The public baseline CSV above is always checked against its own frozen hash. No source contribution is presented as our discovery. ## 5. CPU search with stage-by-stage attribution The baseline is freshly loaded before search. A strictly smaller enclosure is required for admission. Promising MILP candidates receive free-angle sparse LP refinement inherited from the credited CPU implementation. Improvements are transferred by subset selection and integer borders. Fixed seeds determine sampling. Time-limited solver termination may differ across machines. Solver status, binary counts, LP status and the number of stressed contacts are recorded for every attempt. A failed attempt does not prove that no improvement exists. ## 6. Certify the actual submitted decimal strings Unchanged puzzle rows retain their original decimal strings. Changed witnesses receive only centre dilation for a numerical safety gap, never square-size scaling. The unchanged official v17 metric evaluates each changed puzzle, with fallback to its original rows if certification fails. We then validate the whole CSV and a default pandas float64 round trip independently. ## 7. Where did the improvement come from? The score reduction below is incremental over the pinned public portfolio. A zero gain for a stage is a valid negative result. The before/after gallery shows the largest certified improvements; if no new candidate survives, it displays representative inherited witnesses and labels them accordingly. ## Sources, credit and limits - [kmmmvs, Squares Dashboard Public Batch 20261024 V11](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kmmmvs/squares-dashboard-public-batch-20261024?scriptVersionId=361781862): primary pinned public portfolio, SHA-256 `d62a32592633d8093299516433202e879fe5429ac8bc56b28c309e6368a28c5f`. - [Squares in Squares Best Validated Packings](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kmmmvs/squares-in-squares-best-packings): source aggregation, contributor and provenance records. Its reported contributions describe adoption, not exclusive discovery. - [Chris Deotte, FTMC & MILP Refill](https://www.kaggle.com/code/cdeotte/squares-in-squares-ftmc-milp-refill-22-311): tilted-core mutation, exact upright refill and new-basin search, incorporated in the public portfolio. This notebook does not reimplement or claim its FTMC discoveries. - [Alex Chilton, Fault-line DP + Basin Hopping](https://www.kaggle.com/code/alexchilton/fault-line-dp-basin-hopping-lb-22-3079), [Malyshev Danil, Neighbour Transfer + Squeeze](https://www.kaggle.com/code/malyshevdanil/squares-in-squares-neighbour-transfer-squeeze) and the other contributors listed in the retained source tables: inherited portfolio lineage. - [Our Squarecraft II](https://www.kaggle.com/code/avazaku/squarecraft-ii-unjam-the-grid-22-408597-lb): earlier joint contact-switch experiment. - [Kirill Tymchishin, CPU Rectangular Reclosure V2](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-408652-cpu-rectangular-reclosure?scriptVersionId=361218027): primary baseline, SHA-256 pinned; full L-Cut and inherited attribution included. - [Chris Deotte, L-Cut & GPU Squeeze V1](https://www.kaggle.com/code/cdeotte/squares-in-squares-l-cut-gpu-squeeze-22-41?scriptVersionId=361208974): new rectangular L-cut constructions, inherited through the primary baseline. - [Kirill Tymchishin, CPU Separation Graph Reclosure V8](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-472940-cpu-separation-graph-reclosure?scriptVersionId=361188237): pinned public CSV, geometry and CPU refinement helpers, Apache 2.0. - [lightningv08, CUDA Packing Search](https://www.kaggle.com/code/lightningv08/squares-in-squares-cuda-packing-search): prior contact refinement implementation; this notebook uses the credited CPU adaptation. - [kozykappa, Subset transfer, contact refinement and compaction](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kozykappa/subset-transfer-contact-refinement-and-compaction), [Chris Deotte, Multi-Gadget Fault DP](https://www.kaggle.com/code/cdeotte/squares-in-squares-multi-gadget-fault-dp-22-48), and [Alex Chilton](https://www.kaggle.com/code/alexchilton/fault-line-dp-basin-hopping-lb-22-4776): inherited portfolio and construction lineage. - [Francisco Couzo and original discoverers](https://github.com/franciscouzo/square-packing), [Joshua Levy and The Squares Project contributors](https://github.com/jlevy/squares), David Ellsworth, Erich Friedman and original mathematical packing authors: inherited witnesses and their per-witness notices, preserved in `source_provenance/` and `licenses/`. - [Official competition metric V17](https://www.kaggle.com/code/metric/squares-in-squares?scriptVersionId=360167936), unchanged, Apache 2.0. The new experiment uses LP shadow prices and neighbouring contact pressure to select mixed-integer surgery neighbourhoods, followed by inherited refinement and witness transfer. Mixed-integer disjunctive packing optimization and continuous contact optimization are established techniques; no claim is made to invent them or rediscover inherited mathematical packings. `SOURCE_NOTICES.md` preserves the complete inherited credits. The final score is not a proof of global optimality, and search budgets are finite.

Squares in Squares: FTMC + Exact Staircase MILP Refill (fill_rect) + GPU Seam-Welding (22.311627)

Private Technical Briefing: How we jumped from our 22.376289 ensemble baseline down to 22.311627 (–0.06466 LB), why direct full-puzzle perturbations stall on upright zero-modes, and how decoupling the Tilted Core ($T$) from the Upright Staircase Fill ($U$) via exact simplicial reduction + MILP (fill_rect) unlocked 39 rectangular gadget basin jumps in 7.5 minutes (including non-$45^\circ$ packings breaking below the $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.7071$ barrier).

--- ## 1. Why Incremental Full-Puzzle Tweaks Stall — And How `FTMC + fill_rect` Jumps Basins When we audited why local moves on full $N \approx 500\text{--}1000$ packings started saturating around `22.316`, two structural bottlenecks stood out: 1. **Upright Flat Zero-Modes Jam Full-Puzzle Quenching:** In a $K \times K$ puzzle with $n \approx 700$ squares, roughly $500+$ squares are axis-aligned ($0^\circ$) upright blocks. Those upright blocks have over $100$ flat zero-energy sliding modes ("rattlers"). If you apply a large kick or loosen a full puzzle by $2\%$ to jump basins, the upright rows drift slightly out of lattice alignment and jam GPU L-BFGS into a high-bloat local minimum before the tilted core can reorganize. 2. **Two-Ribbon Bottleneck Masking:** In a 2-gadget anti-diagonal packing, the puzzle side length is $L = K + \max(f_1, f_2)$. Even if a radical mutation inside a full puzzle improves Ribbon 1 from $f_1 = 0.92 \to 0.88$, Ribbon 2 is still sitting at $f_2 = 0.92$, so the full puzzle's bounding box $L$ does not shrink at all and the move is rejected! ### The 3-Stage Basin-Jumping Architecture To jump directly between distinct layout basins without upright jamming or second-ribbon masking, we decouple the problem into three stages: * **Stage 1 — Free Tilted Monte Carlo (`FTMC`) in Isolated $(w, h, \Delta m)$ Gadget Space:** Instead of perturbing all squares in a full puzzle, we isolate a single rectangular gadget $(w, h, \Delta m)$ and **strip away 100% of its upright squares**, keeping only the tilted core $T$ ($\sim 15\text{--}120$ tilted squares). On $T$ alone, we apply four macro-mutations: 1. **$\Delta m - 1 \to \Delta m$ Core Insertion:** Take the tighter tilted core $T$ from $(w, h, \Delta m - 1)$, open a slot along the band axis $\vec{u} = (w, h)/\|(w, h)\|$, and insert $+1$ new tilted square directly inside the lozenge. 2. **Boundary-Walk Taper Reshaping:** Walk along the tilted/upright interface, converting $1\text{--}2$ adjacent upright squares into tilted squares (growing a corner bulb) while dropping $1\text{--}3$ tilted squares from the opposite taper tip so an extra staircase row of uprights can fit. 3. **Rational-Slope Non-$45^\circ$ Re-Angling & Shear:** Rotate and shear the tilted band toward rational slopes $\theta \in \{\arctan(1/2)=26.57^\circ,\, 28.07^\circ,\, \arctan(2/3)=33.69^\circ,\, \arctan(3/4)=36.87^\circ,\, 40^\circ,\, 45^\circ\}$. * **Stage 2 — Exact Simplicial + MILP Upright Staircase Refill (`fill_rect`):** Once the mutated tilted core $T_{\text{new}}$ is placed inside $[0, w + f_{\text{try}}] \times [0, h + f_{\text{try}}]$, we **do not guess upright positions**. Instead, `fill_rect(W, H, T_new)` generates: - All 4 wall-anchored integer lattices $\{0.5 + i,\, W - 0.5 - i\} \times \{0.5 + j,\, H - 0.5 - j\}$, **plus** - All **staircase upright candidates** pushed flush against the exact polygon edges of every tilted square in $T_{\text{new}}$ (up to 4 steps deep). - It then applies **exact simplicial corner-rule graph reduction** (resolving $>90\%$ of upright squares in $<0.5\text{ ms}$) followed by per-component **Maximum Independent Set MILP (`scipy.optimize.milp` / HiGHS)** to pack the exact maximum number of non-overlapping upright squares around $T_{\text{new}}$ in $\sim 20\text{ ms}$! * **Stage 3 — GPU Loosen-Then-Squeeze + Seam-Welding & Void-Teleportation:** Because `fill_rect` hands the L40S GPU a crystal-clean seed $T_{\text{new}} \cup U_{\text{exact}}$ with initial overlap $\le 0.022$, batched CUDA L-BFGS (`lbfgs_rect`) + 6-core Sequential LP (`rect_polish`) rapidly quenches the new basin to strict feasibility ($\text{gap} > 10^{-9}$). Improved gadgets are then welded into full $K \times K$ puzzles via **4D Zero-Buffer DP** and **GPU Seam-to-Void Teleportation** (where any colliding square in the shared seam cell $[w_1, w_1+f] \times [h_2, h_2+f]$ is teleported into the largest exact-clearance pocket `exact_holes` near the lozenge tips). --- ## 2. Score Progression (`22.5919` $\to$ `22.3152`) & Per-Band Gain Breakdown The chart below shows our progression across every stage of this campaign, along with the per-band score improvements ($\Delta \text{Score} = \sum_{n \in \text{band}} \Delta L(n)/\sqrt{n}$) from our `22.376289` ensemble baseline down to **`22.311627`**. --- ## 3. Complete Before & After Gallery of All 39 `FTMC + fill_rect` Gadget Basin Jumps (7.5-Minute Run) Below are **all 39 rectangular gadgets** $(w, h, \Delta m)$ where our 7.5-minute run of `gpu_ftmc_rect_basin_jump.py` (`FTMC` Tilted-Core Mutation + `fill_rect` Exact Simplicial/MILP Upright Staircase Refill + GPU L-BFGS + Sequential LP Polish) jumped to a tighter basin, sorted from largest bloat drop ($\Delta f = -0.105950$) to smallest: * **Non-$45^\circ$ Sub-`0.7071` Breakthroughs:** Look closely at **#7 `(6x20+3): 0.746680 -> 0.697181` ($\Delta f = -0.049499$)** and **#8 `(7x22+4): 0.746680 -> 0.703280` ($\Delta f = -0.043400$)**. A $45^\circ$ tilted square has half-extent $1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707107$, which acts as a hard floor for standard $45^\circ$ lozenge crops. By re-angling the tilted band to shallower rational angles ($\sim 26^\circ\text{--}34^\circ$) and refilling the staircase uprights via `fill_rect`, both gadgets broke cleanly **below `0.7071`**! * **Massive Narrow-Ribbon Jumps:** On narrow $w \in \{3, 4\}$ ribbons (**#1 `(3x14+4)` $-0.1060$**, **#2 `(3x14+5)` $-0.0868$**, **#3 `(3x16+5)` $-0.0850$**, **#4 `(3x15+3)` $-0.0693$**, **#5 `(4x21+3)` $-0.0659$**), inserting a tilted square into the $\Delta m - 1$ core or tapering the lozenge tip allowed `fill_rect` to lock an extra upright staircase column along the wall, collapsing the bounding box bloat by $0.05\text{--}0.10$ units! * **High-Surplus DP Leverage Jumps:** Look at **#28 `(7x21+15): 0.956821 -> 0.947566` ($\Delta f = -0.009254$)** and **#31 `(5x14+8): 0.904622 -> 0.899231` ($\Delta f = -0.005391$)** — those single gadget jumps immediately cascaded through our 4D Zero-Buffer DP to improve full puzzles `n=503, 702, 813, 871`! ### Part A: Jumps #1 to #13 ($\Delta f$ from `-0.105950` to `-0.037941`) ### Part B: Jumps #14 to #26 ($\Delta f$ from `-0.037676` to `-0.014105`) ### Part C: Jumps #27 to #39 ($\Delta f$ from `-0.013348` to `-0.000874`, Including High-Surplus DP Winners `#28 (7x21+15)` & `#31 (5x14+8)`) --- ## 4. Full-Puzzle Before vs. After Gallery (`22.376` Ensemble vs. `22.315` Champion) When improved rectangular gadgets are composed across the anti-diagonal fault line via **4D Zero-Buffer DP**, **GPU Seam-Welding + Void-Teleportation**, and **Clean-Compartment Ribbon Grafting**, they transform full $K \times K$ competition puzzles. # Squares in Squares: certified packings for n = 1..1000

Validated unit-square packings for the Kaggle competition *Squares in Squares*, one per puzzle
n = 1..1000, plus the certified best-known index they come from.

## Files

* `index_packings_dilated.csv` - for every count whose best-known side beats the grid (543 of the 1000),
  the exact rational certificate from Francisco Couzo's repository converted to decimal coordinates
  (34 significant digits) with a centre dilation of (1 + 2e-8). The dilation turns every exact contact
  into a gap of at least 2e-8, which the official metric's float64 stage accepts outright; it costs
  about 2e-8 * L on each side. Columns: `n, square_id, x, y, angle` (radians).
* `index_per_n.csv` - the index line for each n: `rounded_up` (the certified side, rounded up to 12
  decimals), `credit` (who found the arrangement, as recorded in the repository), `source`, `status`.
* `certificates/nN.cert` (from version 2 on) - the raw rational witnesses, unchanged: `n S` then one `x y t`
  line per square, `t = tan(theta/2)`. Format and exact verifier by Evan Daniel.
* `constructions_v1.csv` - packings from my own large-n construction search, four variants so far (sub-packings
  composed into bigger containers along a fault line, diagonal ribbon compositions, mixed chains of both, and a
  further chain variant), one block per n in submission format, best of the variants per n; every one passed the exact validator with the 2e-8 margin before it
  went in here.
* `packings_v1.csv` - a complete submission (`id, n, square_id, x, y, angle`): per n, the best of the
  certificate, the grid, and the public Kaggle packings listed below (version 9 of this dataset: the merge of
  2026-10-23 19:30 UTC, which includes Chris Deotte's multi-gadget fault-line packings, the newer public
  packings listed below and my own construction search), after passing a line-by-line mirror
  of the official metric both on the strings as written and after a float64 round trip.
* `per_n_v1.csv` - per n: measured side `L` (50 decimals), `score`, winning `source`, index bound,
  tightest float64 gap and the number of pairs that needed interval arithmetic.

## How it was built

Notebook: https://www.kaggle.com/code/dariushafshar/squares-in-squares-exact-validator-record-merge
(the validator, the merge and the per-band tables are all there). Scores are the competition metric,
sum over n of L/sqrt(n) - 1, lower is better.

## Sources and credits

* Francisco Couzo, franciscouzo/square-packing (MIT), the certificates and the per-n credit lines.
  The MIT notice of that repository (Copyright (c) 2026 Evan Daniel for the verifier; the repository
  licence file) applies to the certificate files redistributed here.
* Evan Daniel, evand/square-packing (MIT): certificate format and exact checker.
* David Ellsworth, Squares in Squares catalogue (https://kingbird.myphotos.cc/packing/squares_in_squares.html),
  continuing Erich Friedman's survey; and the discoverers named in each credit line (Frits Göbel,
  Erich Friedman, David Ellsworth, Thomas Schadt, David W. Cantrell, Károly Hajba, Joost de Winter,
  Evan Daniel, Darius Muglich, PingYou Ltd, Mykhailo Polkovskyi, M.Z. Arslanov, S.A. Mustafin and
  Z.K. Shangitbayev, and others).
* Joshua Levy and contributors, The Squares Project (https://github.com/jlevy/squares), the open register
  most of the recent records went through.
* Public Kaggle packings in `packings_v1.csv` (rows marked by `source` in `per_n_v1.csv`): Chris Deotte,
  *Ensemble*, *L-Cut & GPU Squeeze* and *Multi-Gadget Fault DP* (anti-diagonal fault-line composition of gadgets);
  Janus (jiwasawa), *D4 Seam DP Dual GPU LBFGS*; Aqib Raza, *Top LB Blending + Visualization*;
  Кирилл Тымчишин, *CPU Separation Graph Reclosure*; Kozykorpesh, *Subset transfer, contact refinement and compaction*; alex chilton,
  *Fault-line DP + Basin Hopping* and *Certified Merge of Public Packings*; SeshuRaju, *1000 Puzzles - Ensemble*;
  Malyshev Danil, *Neighbour Transfer + Squeeze*; Кирилл Тымчишин, *CPU Window Closure + Contact Polish*;
  Vladislav Lavrentev, *CUDA Packing Search*; and the earlier work they build on by avazaku and prvsiyan.

Everything here is an upper bound. No record claim is made for any n.

Licence of this compilation: CC BY 4.0. Certificate files keep their MIT licence.

## 5. Recompose the updated gadgets on CUDA

A crop with footprint w×h and surplus d contains w·h+d unit squares in a box (w+f)×(h+f). Along a staircase fault, several such gadgets add their surpluses while sharing a container excess controlled by the **largest f**. Reusing a better donor can therefore improve multiple puzzles.

CUDA C++ computes crop order statistics, conservative separating-line tip profiles and the minimax DAG search. Quantized support bounds protect joins; unit-row or unit-column buffers provide alternative transitions. Reflection and transposition cover all eight symmetries. The second pass uses the newly certified construction bank. Independent full SAT screening precedes official decimal admission; the GPU's geometric estimate is not reported as a certified score.

SQUARES IN SQUARES

CUDA Packing Search

Change the core · Refill the grid · Reuse the geometry

**Certified score: 22.307818650783. Lower is better.** The useful unit of search is a reusable rectangular gadget. A new arrangement can improve several puzzle sizes once it is composed with other gadgets. This version combines fresh, credited public witnesses with CUDA support-profile composition, then crops the new compositions and composes again. Default **Run All** replays a frozen CSV, displays the measured gains and checks all 1,000 score terms on CPU. Optional CUDA search is disabled. All squares keep side one. ## 1. Account for the source of every gain The score is $\sum_{n=1}^{1000}(L_n/\sqrt{n}-1)$. The official scorer supplies the upright-grid fallback when a puzzle is omitted. A smaller floating bounding box is only a proposal: each accepted replacement passes the official interval geometry checks on raw decimal strings and after ordinary pandas float64 parsing. The refreshed portfolio retains 60 better witnesses from Sung Heo's public output, which itself preserves its contributors' credits. Malyshev Danil's newer output adds no further wins after that union. Chris Deotte's tilted-core constructions supply the earlier large jump. The two CUDA rows below measure additional certified gain over this refreshed union, not ownership of the input constructions. Tracing every winning chain shows that none uses the newly mutated nightly worker archive. The additional CUDA gain comes from recomposing retained/public donors, chiefly n=503. The night archive remains available for inspection, but its 59 local gadget improvements are not presented as useful portfolio discoveries. ## 2. Change structure before squeezing Full-puzzle L-BFGS can spend most of its effort on upright squares that slide inside the same arrangement. Following Chris Deotte's FTMC briefing, strip those squares out and mutate the tilted core: coherent re-angle/shear, insertion, taper deletion, boundary exchange, archive crossover, and rational-slope lattice starts. Refill the upright area, then squeeze the complete gadget. Bulk row/column refill runs in CUDA. A small number of near-capacity failures reach the finite-candidate conflict graph and bounded HiGHS MILP. FP32 screens many proposals; FP64, gap repair and the unchanged official interval metric guard acceptance. This is not an exact solver for the continuous packing problem. The saved T4 campaign evaluated more than six million core proposals and accepted 59 gadget improvements. Its final portfolio stayed at its starting union: a local gadget gain is not automatically a global score gain, and the earlier composition stage encountered a CuPy unsigned-sentinel conversion error. The replay below includes the corrected, tested composer and the saved gadget archive. For a chain of gadgets, $L=K+max_i f_i$. Improving a gadget below the active maximum can leave the score unchanged. Fresh public experiments by Alex Chilton also show that exact-construction gadgets can stay rigid. Spend search on numerical bottlenecks that occur in useful chains, and retain alternative support profiles even when their isolated bounding box is slightly worse. ## 3. Compose, re-crop, compose again A gadget holds $wh+d$ unit squares in $(w+f)\times(h+f)$. CUDA enumerates all eight symmetries and records occupied-corner support bounds at **30°, 45° and 60°**. Incoming and outgoing separators can differ. The staircase DP keeps footprint, surplus, outgoing normal and support bin, minimizing the largest fractional excess. Prefix minima prune profiles dominated by another profile with no greater excess, no larger outgoing support and no smaller incoming support. This dominance is exact for the finite conservative profile table. Every reconstructed packing is checked geometrically and certified separately. The first pass uses 24 support bins. Its newly composed layouts become donors for a second 32-bin pass: a useful compound arrangement can now be cropped into a different gadget. The larger profile table reduces quantization loss, while the new donor set changes the available composition structures. These effects are combined in this experiment and should not be presented as an isolated resolution ablation. ## 4. Look at the accepted arrangements Both panels use the same scale. Blue squares are tilted; grey squares are nearly upright. Small numerical changes can be invisible, so the measured container side accompanies each drawing. ## 5. Readable implementation and bounded optional search The archive restores the Python orchestration, CUDA C++ kernels, official metric and original source notices. The frozen default uses CPU only. Enable the optional branch on an NVIDIA GPU with CuPy and PyTorch; it starts from the certified file and uses a 12-minute hard process limit. Search proposals are admitted only after certification. No competition submission is made by the notebook. ## 6. Certify the serialized output Both checks include submitted witnesses and every omitted puzzle's official grid fallback. Interval overlap or an uncertifiable contact rejects the candidate. GPU floating-point precision is a search tool; this independent final check determines admission. ## Credits [Chris Deotte](https://www.kaggle.com/code/cdeotte/squares-in-squares-ftmc-milp-refill-22-311): tilted-core/refill architecture, public gadget examples, staircase composition. [Sung Heo](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kmmmvs/squares-dashboard-public-batch-20261024): refreshed portfolio with inherited per-source credits. [Alex Chilton](https://www.kaggle.com/code/alexchilton/fault-line-dp-basin-hopping-lb-22-3079): leverage-ranked gadget experiments and repeated composition. [Malyshev Danil](https://www.kaggle.com/code/malyshevdanil/squares-in-squares-neighbour-transfer-squeeze): neighbour-transfer and propagation experiments. Avazaku, Kirill Tymchishin, Dariush Afshar, Evan Daniel, Francisco Couzo, Joshua Levy, David Ellsworth, Erich Friedman, prvsiyan, and all contributors listed in the Layout Atlas and the preserved notices retain their mathematical, code and witness credits. Public witnesses are not claimed as new discoveries here. `refresh_SOURCE_NOTICES.md` and `refresh_sungheo_NOTICES.md` preserve source hashes, lineage and licensing context. # Sources and changes

The frozen starting submission is Vladislav Lavrentev (lightningv08),
Squares in Squares | CUDA Packing Search, version 6 / native version 360946057:
https://www.kaggle.com/code/lightningv08/squares-in-squares-cuda-packing-search?scriptVersionId=360946057
Baseline CSV SHA-256: 2ab6ab746b5ab0fdf14f8f9eb86da3ce052b651803d65009cbef2d12530c7aac
Baseline official v17 score: 22.595460848551.

The new contribution is a CPU experiment applying exhaustive translated-window
queries to the latest portfolio, followed by contact refinement with changed
regularization/trust settings and propagation across puzzle sizes. Segment-tree
window sweeps, cross-size transfer and contact polishing already occur in the
credited source lineage; these primitives are not claimed as new inventions.
cpu_contact_polish.py is adapted from lightningv08's Apache-2.0 contact_polish.py.
Changes remove CUDA imports, expose trust/regularization parameters, and use the
local CPU geometry/repair implementation. The other experiment modules are
written for this experiment. No new world-record or global-optimality claim.

The baseline inherits numerical layouts from avazaku's Squarecraft, prvsiyan's
A Square Deal, alexchilton's Thinking Outside the Grid and Certified Merge,
David Ellsworth's catalogue and Erich Friedman's collection, Joshua Levy and
contributors' Squares Project, Francisco Couzo and individually credited
contributors, and Darius Muglich. Original discoverers, construction and solver
authors retain credit, including de Winter, Fang, Daniel, Göbel, Cantrell,
Bidwell, Hajba and Schadt. The frozen attribution files are retained under
source_provenance/. Mathematical coordinates are modified by subset selection,
rotations, contact refinement, centre dilation and integer border addition.

Primary snapshots and grants:
https://github.com/jlevy/squares/tree/970e89de8c253133500797b414d2dd31f9e17258
https://github.com/franciscouzo/square-packing/tree/7b6c87e129cf80b5ff9847b90b47fd30b4563c54/certificates/best
https://github.com/jlevy/squares/issues/686#issuecomment-6302118274
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
https://kingbird.myphotos.cc/packing/squares_in_squares.html
https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/lightningv08/squares-in-squares-layout-atlas

The official metric is an unchanged Apache-2.0 copy of Kaggle Competition
Metrics, version 17 / native version 360167936:
https://www.kaggle.com/code/metric/squares-in-squares?scriptVersionId=360167936
Metric SHA-256: 312458227c78f56bd5e2eec3dc5fbb8787989422bbf72ce66c3c290048e89733

Inherited source licenses and original authorship are preserved. This notebook
does not redistribute source research prose, SVG artwork, or third-party images.
